catalog_quote: [3.6] There is no rigorous phonological difference between clitics, suffixes, and postposed particles such as postpositions. Stress and accent patterns, which in other languages of the world often bring out cliticization, are not relevant to Nanga. ... [2.1] Nanga has a typical Dogon stem-level tonal system, with at least one (lexical) high tone element per stem. At the level of syllables, tones are H[igh], L[ow], <HL> (falling), <LH> (rising), and bell-shaped <LHL>. There are no <HLH> syllables. ... Verb stems are lexically /LH/ or /H/. ... Several suffixes impose specific tone overlays on the preceding stem, overriding lexical tones. ... [3.2.2] Segmental phonological rules generally point to a trochaic bias, i.e. bisyllabic [sw] with a strong followed by a weak. audit.reasoning: The coding 'tonal, no stress rule' rests on the only existing description of Nanga, a 444-page 2016 reference grammar by the language's sole documenter, which we hold and whose deciding sentences ('Stress and accent patterns... are not relevant to Nanga'; 'typical Dogon stem-level tonal system'; 'trochaic bias' from segmental rules only) are confirmed verbatim at the cited pages. Glottolog lists no other descriptive work; web search turned up only tonosyntax studies (McPherson 2014 diss., fetched sources; McPherson & Heath 2016 NLLT) that reuse Heath's data and are silent on word stress. Nothing better exists and nothing suggests the coding is wrong.

sources.citation: McPherson, Laura E. 2014. Replacive grammatical tone in the Dogon languages. PhD dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles. 370 pp.
sources.quote: Treats Nanga as a lexical+replacive grammatical tone language ('Nanga is one of the most tonosyntactically complex languages in the sample', p. 163); data explicitly from Heath's grammar drafts. No statement on Nanga word stress; the only 'stress' discussion (sec. 2.7.2, p. 118) is a diachronic speculation that Dogon tonal overlays originated in phrasal de-emphasis, not a synchronic stress claim.
